bar: This is the number one rule for your set
note:
REGRETS EQUALS REDEMPTION

JUSTICE.Reasonable Doubt, Jay-Z’s first album, came out in 1996. I was just graduating and heading to Los Angeles to begin the post-college chapter of my life. I was grown – or at least I thought I was – and ready to see what life had to offer me. I remember listening to “Regrets” on a cassette tape I made to listen to while on the 4-hour plane ride. I remember rewinding the song over and over because this rule of learning to live with regrets kept challenging me to think about a life that was ahead of me that I knew deep down could go one of two ways: south, and heading back home to momma to try it again, or north, and heading back home to momma having achieved something worthwhile while living on my own in the City of Angels. I was afraid. And on that plane I contemplated coming back to Atlanta where my comfort zone was safe. Two things stuck with me. Just before I boarded that plane for LA, my mom told me “don’t take no wooden nickels because you can’t buy anything with them”, and Jay-Z rapping over and over about this rule of learning to “live with regrets.” Learn to live with regrets. Don’t take no wooden nickels. Don’t take no wooden nickels. Learn to live with regrets. Huh? In my twenty-something year old mind, I didn’t want regrets. And I damn sure didn’t want money made outta wood. I just wanted rewards. All this wisdom was scaring me!! Eventually it hit me. Paired together, my mom’s words with Jay-Z’s brought me some piece of mind. (At least enough to not hop back on the plane heading home to Georgia.)

“To get ahead in life mistakes are inevitable. And oftentimes mistakes become regrets. But remember to take care of yourself, and if you try as best as possible to make careful decisions then the regrets stay at bay.” This is how I rationalized it. I carried this with me then, and I carry it with me now. Mistakes I’ve made. Plenty of them. However, I’ve learned that out of the mistakes come redemption and forgiveness. Therein lies the justice of regrets

The Daily Dose of Realness: In Decoded (2010), Jay-Z says that “Regrets” was the last song on the album because “It’s the last feeling you have before you go to sleep or feel when you wake up and look at yourself in the bathroom mirror” (265). Mistakes bring about regrets, and regrets can be a heavy burden. That’s life though. The silver lining is that regrets create a space for forgiveness and personal redemption, both of which neutralize any heaviness. Both of which are necessary on the road to success. That’s the number one rule to survival a la Shawn Carter. The number two rule is don’t take no wooden nickels a la my mommy dearest. Take care of yourself. Take care of others. Godspeed

Jimmy Hoffa was last seen at 2:45pm on July 30, 1975, at a restaurant in the Bloomfield Terrace of Detroit. He was reported missing by his wife after Hoffa did not return “back home.”

The suspected killers were thought to be tied to the Italian Mafia as well as the fledgling Teamsters union. Hoffa’s body was never found, leading to one of the world’s most notable conspiracy theory topics.

bar: We don't know a word to a verse, all we know is the chorus
note:
This section further elaborates on the idea presented before it. That we as the listeners are to blame for this trend of simple, dumbed down music, and the market will keep producing it as long as we keep listening.

Eminem emphasizes this point clear as day in this section. He describes the relationship between a hit Pop song and the average music listener. In these three lines, we are able to see both cause and effect in the vicious cycle of music production and success.

These three lines can be viewed as somewhat of a circle. With no particular start and end point, and that is the point. We as a people listen to the chorus, not the verses, the Chorus now center stage repeats itself so we can remember it, and finally, we love the song. Each of these three lines could be placed in any order that is what makes this section so powerful. Eminem is describing a circle, a circle that will never stop unless it is broken.

While we can argue for days over the philosophy of a changing human race towards sound bites, constant stimulation and the overall effect these have on our psychology. I believe the message is simpler than that. I think that the message Eminem is trying to convey in this section and throughout this entire song is that we as the listener must overcome this circle ourselves.  While it may take time or even some work to find someone we enjoy listening too, if we give up and accept low effort cash-grab songs we will kill real music with no one else to blame but ourselves.

While I realize this song specifically deals with the effect of this low effort trend on Hip Hop. I believe that it pertains to the entire music industry. For more information and another interesting take on this very same idea, I would highly recommend the song Repeat Stuff, by comic/musician Bo Burnham. The talks about the effects of corporate built Pop/Love songs designed to appeal to young people, be catchy and be memorable. The song itself is a satirical interpretation of a corporate built love song and is both very funny and dark at the same time. I cannot recommend it enough even if you just want to laugh.

other_notes.note:
Here we see Eminem further explore the themes of simplicity in music and ignorance in audience first defined in the section above this one. These two themes remain predominant both throughout the entire song and the changing artist interpretations.

Even though these two themes will be a predominant focus for the entire song, this section primarily fixates on the second theme, complacency, and ignorance of the audience. Eminem (as per his style) wastes no time in presenting his feelings on the matter, describing the average music consumer who is more interested in getting drunk, hearing simple beats from pop songs and picking up chicks than actually listening to the music.

This is not the first time that Eminem has voiced his anger at current music trends, but perhaps this song is his most direct stance on the subject. Hip Hop artists and fans often voice similar concerns, condemning music that follows this beat-heavy trend. Few, however, are able to fully summarize, label and demonstrate this trend as comic/musician Bo Burnham. In his “Make Happy” tour Bo Burnham labels this changing genre as “Beat Fetishism”, where words and songwriting are traded in for a “sick beat.” He then continues on to satirize the practice by rapping Little Teapot and Baa Baa Blacksheep over a “sick beat.” Video below.

Perhaps the most important thing to take away from this section is not an anger at the music industry or frustration at artists who use these techniques but to realize that the problem stems from us, the listener. This is elaborated further in the next section in the song directly below this one.

JAY-Z mentions the late Floridian rapper XXXTENTACION, who was murdered at a motorsport shop in Deerfield Beach, Florida on June 18th, 2018.

He compares the murder of the young rapper to the case of George Zimmermann, a Florida man who became infamous for the killing of unarmed black teen, Trayvon Martin, in which he claimed self-defense based on Florida’s ‘Stand your ground’ law. He was found not guilty of second degree murder in a trial by jury. The Black Panthers put a $10,000 bounty on his head, but he remains alive today, allegedly boasting about killing Trayvon.

With these bars, Jay is voicing his frustration with both the state and citizens of Florida: they let a young rapper die a premature death, but couldn’t put an end to a man who murdered an unarmed black teen.

Since the murder of Martin, Jay has connected with his family and lent them both financial and emotional support. In July 2018 Hov’s latest docuseries production, Rest in Power: The Trayvon Martin Story will premiere on the Paramount Network.

bar: Niggas thought they was ill, found out they was ill
note:
Hov is saying “People thought they were on my level, thought they were ‘ill’ like me but they found out they were really sick in a bad way, outmatched and overwhelmed. I set the tone so perfectly, it’s like I controlled how they felt. I played the game so well, they reacted exactly how I intended.”

Jay-Z is using a play on the word ill, which in hip hop slang can mean cool, dope, or skilled, but also literally means sick or weak. He’s saying they thought they were dope, but they were actually in over their heads. And the second line shows his calculated dominance, his ability to not just outperform, but manipulate perception and emotion.

Also this works as a triple entendre:


“Ill” as in dope: They thought they were raw, talented, on his level.
“Ill” as in sick: They were actually messed up, weak, not built for the game.
“Eel” which ties to the “eww” as in a slimy, spineless creature: A metaphor for suckers, snakes, or fake people, slippery and untrustworthy. He’s saying they’re not just not ill, they’re bottom-feeders.



That subtle pronunciation flip from ill to eel creates that extra diss, not just that they were wrong about themselves, but that they’re lowlife types trying to swim with sharks.

Jay’s genius is that he never says “eel” outright, but he makes you hear it. That’s wordplay at its finest.

vault_lines: Niggas thought they was ill, found out they was ill

2) wet from “sweating” – slang for copying – his style.

This latter interpretation is an elegant nod to Eric B. & Rakim’s legendary “Don’t Sweat the Technique,” which essentially means “don’t copy the style.”



These two interpretations of “wet,” along with the aforementioned “blood” interpretation when reading “check out” to refer to murder, set up “wet, when you check out” as a bona fide triple entendre.

Firstly, when he adds that the technique is from the “2 Tecs” (e.g., two 9-Tec guns), this makes the “technique” refer to shooting. bar: Rucker game attender with the Bent parked
note:
Jay likes to remind people that, despite what they might have heard to the contrary, his status in the hood is still firmly intact, which he does here with with a couple of basketball references.

Rucker Park is a basketball court in Harlem, famous as a streetball venue. Over the years it has served as both a breeding ground for and sideline attraction to a host of NBA talent.



Despite his wealth and fame, you’re perfectly likely to find Hov there, taking in a game. The fact that he’s in attendance will be easily evidenced by the brand new Bentley (identifiable by the temporary dealership plates still hanging from it) that he’s left outside, parked right there on the curb!

The implication here is that he’s so confident in the level of respect he commands in the streets that he thinks nothing of leaving a car worth several hundreds of thousands of dollars parked up in Harlem, the notion that it might get stolen doesn’t even occur to him.

Similarly, you’re just as likely to catch him front and centre at a Knicks game, jewellery on display for all to see. Whilst courtside at the Garden is a decidedly more upscale setting than Rucker Park his point remains the same; he’s right there in clear view, not hiding from anyone.

Interestingly, the year following this songs release Jay would actually enter his own, star-studded team into Rucker Park’s Entertainer’s Basketball Classic tournament,  counting a just-drafted prospect by the name of Lebron James amongst his ranks.



He came tantalisingly close to unseating fellow New York emcee, and one-time rival, Fat Joe’s Terror Squad team for the title, but was ultimately derailed when the 2003 New York blackout coincided with his sides final, potentially championship winning game.

bar: Sucker free, no shuckin' me, I don't jive turkey
note:
Here Jay-Z is referring to two sayings “shuck and jive” and “jive turkey.” The phrase shuck and jive was used throughout the 1920s (maybe earlier) to refer to someone who makes statements only meant to deceive when asked about their work/work ethic. For example, when someones manager/boss asks “what are you doing?” someone could shuck and jive around the answer in order to appear busy. It is for this reason that he also references not being a jive turkey because this is a term used throughout the 70s to describe people who made empty promises or were full of talk. It was referenced in a song by the Ohio Players and also on the shows “The Jeffersons” and “Good Times” which helped to popularize it.



By making these references Jay-Z is stating that he doesn’t have anyone around him who operates like a sucka and more importantly it isn’t possible to fool him specifically because he doesn’t engage in “jive turkey behavior.” His word is his bond.

https://twitter.com/kanyewest/status/1068611802030698496

Kanye famously tweeted pictures of himself wearing Trump’s signature “Make America Great Again” hat. In a 2018 interview on The Van Jones Show, Jay expressed disappointment with Trump’s presidency, as well as his “shit-hole” comment regarding African countries. He also convinced Meek Mill to cancel a White House meeting with Trump, and theorized that Trump’s contentious behavior might bring the conversation about systemic racism in America to the forefront.

Additionally, these lines touch on the media’s tendency to pit legendary artists like Prince and Michael Jackson against each other. On the contrary, Jay has made his love for Kanye quite clear:

–From My Next Guest Needs No Introduction with David Letterman

Moreover, “Prince” is the name of Michael Jackson’s first-born son, so the “Michael and Prince’s DNA” line may not only be a parallel between the pitting of black artists against one another, but also a reference to the practice of family separation during American slavery. Historically, some African slaves that worked in the house associated themselves with their slave master, rather than field slaves. As Jay said on “The Story Of OJ”:

House nigga, don’t fuck with me
I’m a field nigga, go shine cutlery

Lastly, Jay insinuates that both his estate and his spouse, Beyoncé, are superior to Trump’s wife and property. Ironically, from 2007 to 2017, Jay rented an apartment from President Trump.

“Steam” is a double entendre. First, he references drugs and the smoke (or “steam”) that comes from smoking drugs like heroin. He is referencing the idea that many people get high to dull the pain and struggled associated with poverty. This imagery also calls back to the line about China White heroin, and how it allows its users to “take flight.”

“Steam” is also a reference to the anger those in poverty feel toward people who are more affluent. When someone is mad, they’re often described as “steaming hot.”



Finally, he transitions to the next couplet with a reference to the Devil, who lives in a place consumed by fire. Thus being “close to the Devil” would make a kettle “steam.”

The term O.G. is the acronym for Original Gangster with the roots dating back to 1972 when Original was used by the Crips. It was used to insinuate that “we’re first”, the Originals. Two years later the word “Gangster” was added to form the Original Gangster Crips and they only used the term “O.G.” when writing their name or their neighbourhood.

Since then, the term O.G. has been widely used in hip-hop and hood culture in reference to original individuals within a certain area or just someone successful or highly skilled in any given area.

Rick Ross shares more of his wisdom with us in his verse on Ima Boss where he mentions how an O.G. is someone who can take care of themselves, who can achieve success in a certain field. Whereas a boss (pronounced “bawse” by Rick Ross) is someone who guarantees all their boys eat.

To expand this further, the term eat is used to describe success in such a way that everyone reaps and benefits from it. The prime example of this as always is a figure such as Jay-Z, who throughout the years has guaranteed quite a few people gon’ eat.

other_notes.note:
Meek Mill uses clever wordplay to explain the process of disloyalty by those in his inner circle.

First, he warns the listener to be hesitant on telling people where they live. They can appear “where you land.” This can mean your city, or residence. Once they are with you they will put that “hammer” in your face and rob you. The term hammer references a handgun, it comes from older style pistols especially revolvers with an exposed component called a hammer. To ask for the cake is to ask for his jewelry; Cake usually has icing on it, ice is another popular slang term for jewels with so many diamonds on them that they literally shine like ice.

Lastly Meek explains how those around him keep falling away from his side. His dogs, a title used to express brotherhood have switched into snakes. Snakes are referenced as sneaky, untrustworthy, and deceptive. Even worse is when these same snakes turn to rats; These are people who openly snitch on their previous brothers to the authorities. Meek says in his last line how he has been running through the jungle which hosts all sorts of dangerous animals, including rats and snakes.


Pictured above: Hammer component on Smith & Wesson firearm.

note:
Cutting a deck refers to the procedure where the dealer completes the shuffle, and then sets the cards face-down on the table near the designated player, typically the player to the dealer’s right. The player cuts the deck by removing a contiguous range of cards from the deck, and places them toward himself so that the stack of cards to be dealt is closest to the dealer.

In this case, Meek’s the dealer, and he’s not dealing cards.. he’s dealing coke. Cutting a brick of cocaine refers to diluting the drug to increase its weight and maximize profit.

Also, note the wordplay on shuffle and cut it, since Meek is clearly not in the dope game anymore. He’s “cutting” songs, and a popular option for any playback device is the “shuffle” option. Playing off of the long running trope of comparing making music to making dope, like Kanye previously said in his song “Crack Music”.

Here Justin calls out “cancel culture,” which is a modern phenomenon where people are condemned and often boycotted for a misdeed (whether past or present) by others on social media and often results in deleterious affects on a person’s professional and/or social spheres.

For example, James Gunn, the director of 2014 film Guardians of the Galaxy, was called out in July 2018 for tweets he had made ten years prior and was then fired by Disney. His position was later reinstated after public outcry, but many people who have experienced similar backlash have not been so lucky.

Justin sees the very essence of “cancel culture” as the antithesis of repentance and forgiveness, themes he explores on both Freedom. and on previous songs of his such as November 2015’s “Life Is Worth Living” where he sang:

My reputation’s on the line

He questions whether this type of response to people’s actions does society any good as it never gives the room for a person to make mistakes, learn from them and therefore, better themselves.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N8H3i1HFYuM

Justin Bieber confronting the paparazzi after being filmed

bar: I just wanna flex her, flex her, flex her
note:
In these lines, Kodak uses high-stakes, figurative language to describe his desire for a committed relationship.


The Motivation: Kodak admits his frustration (“so fuckin' mad”) that his previous “Push-Pull” game almost caused the girl to leave for good. This realization acts as the catalyst for him dropping his “casual” persona.
The Metaphors: Terms like “kidnap,” “trap,” and “bag” are used figuratively here to mean “locking her down” or making her his exclusive partner. In this context, “trapping” her isn’t about restriction, but about securing the relationship so she doesn’t “get away” again.
The Lifestyle Shift: He contrasts “casual” dating with “fly dates on private planes.” This signifies a move from low-effort “situationships” to a high-level, serious partnership where he is willing to invest both his emotions and his wealth.



By using such strong terminology, Kodak emphasizes that his attraction is no longer a “game"—it has become an obsession with ensuring she stays in his life permanently.

bar: I just wish that Jessica could just forgive me
note:
In these lines, Kodak addresses a specific woman named Jessica, pleading for her forgiveness. However, the line concludes with a clever phonetic play on words.

When spoken aloud, “Jess” sounds nearly identical to “Yes.” By placing it immediately after the phrase “all I ask for,” Kodak creates a double meaning:


The Direct Appeal: He is calling out to “Jess” specifically, making the plea personal and urgent.
The Desired Answer: He is literally stating that a “Yes” is “all he asks for” in response to his request for a second chance.



This technique allows Kodak to show vulnerability while maintaining the wordplay-heavy style he is known for, turning a simple name into the very answer he’s hoping to hear.

bar: Ten bodies or less, you a fuckin' queen (And it's fat)
note:
In this sequence, 21 Savage humorously codifies a woman’s sexual history into a mock hierarchy of worthiness, blending sexual bravado with satirical commentary. On the surface, he’s establishing arbitrary thresholds: ten or fewer partners earns respect (“queen”), fewer than nine implies casual intimacy without protection, and fewer than eight elevates her to marriageable status. The rapid shifts in these criteria exaggerate how absurd and contradictory the fixation on sexual pasts can be, turning a common trope in hip-hop into a deliberately over-the-top joke.

This passage also reveals something deeper about 21 Savage’s commentary on masculinity and sexual politics in rap. He’s simultaneously flaunting dominance and control—deciding who’s “worthy” and who’s not—while satirizing the often hypocritical and performative ways men measure women’s value. The specificity of the numbers (“ten,” “nine,” “eight”) gives the bar a pseudo-scientific absurdity, as if he’s presenting a serious formula, which contrasts hilariously with the ridiculousness of the content.

Additionally, the lines reflect the album’s broader tone in POP IT and What Happened to the Streets?—a mix of excessive flexing, humor, and social commentary. By openly quantifying sexual experience, 21 Savage highlights the inherent absurdity of these standards while still flexing sexual dominance, showing how trap music often blends threat, desire, and satire into a single punchline. The humor, exaggeration, and bravado all work together to make this bar memorable, shocking, and culturally resonant, capturing both the playfulness and the critique embedded in modern trap lyricism.

This bar also connects to the way Latto is always talking about her low body count, that’s where this wordplay comes from. He’s actually complimenting her. 21 frequently hyperbolizes experiences of wealth, sex, and violence, using extreme imagery to assert power while signaling self-awareness about the performative nature of these claims. The result is a line that functions on multiple levels: a sexual flex, a satirical jab at cultural obsessions with women’s pasts, and a testament to 21 Savage’s ability to combine humor with menace seamlessly.

note:
In this opening passage, 21 Savage delivers what many scholars consider the definitive modern meditation on affirmation. While casual listeners may mistake these repeated “yeahs” as simple ad-libs, closer analysis reveals a masterclass in minimalistic expression.

By saying yeah four times — and then daring to say yeah again — 21 challenges the boundaries of language itself. Each “yeah” is identical in spelling, pronunciation, and meaning, a poetic symmetry so precise that it borders on mathematical perfection. Some critics argue this sequence rivals the structural economy of Hemingway; others place it closer to postmodern existentialism, where meaning is found in repetition, not variation.

The subtle shift from “yeah” to “ye-yeah” represents what many interpret as Savage’s commentary on the instability of identity in late-stage capitalism — a linguistic flourish so daring that few contemporary writers would attempt it.

Just as a tiger is exotic in America but not India, the label of exotic cannabis depends on the location and audience. To a newbie, almost anything with a high THC count and colorful trichome crystals will feel exotic. But the term does not traditionally describe familiar favorites like OG Kush, Sour Diesel or Jack Herer.

The name suggests origins in the tropics or Middle East, but for many it is nothing more than a marketing tool used to classify ambiguous but potent strains whose true genealogy is unknown to the dealer.

A supplier offering an exotic strain could have anything from a fruity sativa to a dark purple indica, but the general standard for the name is a top-shelf strain that is both rare for the region and has extremely noticeable effects. (Leafly)

bar: Goin' both sides, yeah, you could say I'm B-I (Hey, hey)
note:
Cassette tapes and vinyl records are double-sided to increase the music quantity that can fit on a single strand of tape and vinyl disk respectfully. One side is called A and the other is named B. Tyler saying he is ‘B’ is a metaphor for having gone through both sides, as Side B on tapes and records tends to contain the latter half of album/mixtape/compilation implying he’s already been through Side A.

Tyler loves talking about his bisexuality in his music. Bisexual people tend to shorten their sexuality’s namesake to ‘Bi’ to pertain their sexual attraction towards both sexes as Tyler has done by pronouncing both letters in the slang term, “B-I”, allowing the metaphor for binary characteristics of cassettes and vinyl records and bisexuality to be married in a single line.

The cassette and vinyl record media reference extends Tyler’s appreciation for the formats. He has commercially released cassettes and vinyls for Wolf in 2013, Flower Boy in 2017, IGOR in 2019 and CALL ME IF YOU GET LOST in 2021, while also releasing vinyl records for Goblin in 2011 and Cherry Bomb in 2015 and a re-edition in 2020).

Traditionally, cassettes and vinyls would keep promotional-focused music on Side A with the hope of radio airtime. Side B would typically contain music to receive less attention. Tyler’s discography being released during the digital age of music rendered the aforementioned logistics of double sided music media less prevalent. Contemporary releases of albums perceive Side B as a means to fit more high-quality audio onto a single tape or record.
